title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
hints: preorder always visits a subtree's root before anything else in that subtree - so what does the very first element of any preorder slice tell you?

once you know the root's value, find it in the corresponding inorder slice - everything to its left in that slice is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree, and you know their sizes
use those sizes to slice the remaining preorder elements too: the next (left subtree size) elements of preorder (after the root) build the left subtree, and the rest build the right subtree

precompute a map from value to index in the full inorder array before recursing, so finding the split point is O(1) instead of a linear scan each time - then write the resulting values into the output array at the correct heap-index position, filling gaps with -101 and trimming the trailing sentinel-only tail
commonMistakes: re-scanning the inorder array linearly for the root's position on every recursive call instead of precomputing a lookup, which is correct but needlessly slow
miscomputing the size of the left subtree slice, causing the preorder array to be split at the wrong point for the right subtree

writing values into the output array using a running index counter instead of the actual heap-index formula (2*i+1, 2*i+2), which produces a structurally wrong array even if the values are all correct

content.problemStatement:
Binary trees are encoded as flat arrays using complete-binary-tree
(heap) indexing:

- the root sits at index 0
- a node at index `i` has its left child at index `2*i+1` and right child at index `2*i+2`
- a position at or beyond the array's end, or one holding the sentinel `-101`, means "no node there"
- real node values are always between -100 and 100, so -101 never collides with a genuine value

For example, `[1, 2, 3, -101, 4]` encodes this tree:

```
      1
     / \
    2   3
     \
      4
```

Node 2's left child is missing (index 3 is -101) and its right child is 4 (index 4).

You're given two arrays describing the same tree: `preorder`, its preorder
traversal (node, then left subtree, then right subtree), and `inorder`,
its inorder traversal (left subtree, then node, then right subtree). All
values in the tree are distinct.

**Reconstruct the tree and return it in the heap-index array format described above.**

When building the output array, fill any internal gaps with -101, but do not pad past the last real node needed to represent the full shape, trim trailing sentinel positions off the very end of the array.
constraints: preorder and inorder consist of distinct values
inorder is guaranteed to be a valid inorder traversal of the same tree that preorder is a valid preorder traversal of
notes: empty input (preorder and inorder both empty), which should produce a tree representing no nodes
a tree that is entirely a left chain or entirely a right chain, exercising the trimming rule

sampleTestCases.explanation: 3 is the root (first in preorder). in inorder, everything before 3 (just [9]) is the left subtree, everything after (15, 20, 7) is the right subtree. the left subtree is a single leaf 9. the right subtree has root 20 (next in preorder after skipping the left subtree), with left child 15 and right child 7
1 is the root. in inorder, 2 comes before 1, so 2 is entirely in the left subtree. 1 has no right child, so the array is trimmed after index 1

1 is the root. in inorder, nothing comes before 1, so the left subtree is empty; everything after (2, 3) is the right subtree. that right subtree's root is 2 (next in preorder), and within it, nothing comes before 2 in [2, 3], so 2 also has an empty left subtree and a right child of 3

optimal.time: O(n) with a hash map from value to its index in inorder for O(1) root-splitting lookups
optimal.space: O(n) for the value-to-index map, output array, and recursion stack
optimal.pattern: recursive divide and conquer: the first element of preorder is always the current subtree's root, and its position in inorder splits the remaining elements into left and right subtree ranges

bruteForce.approach: same recursive divide-and-conquer idea, but re-searching inorder linearly for the root's position each time instead of precomputing a value-to-index lookup
bruteForce.time: O(n^2) worst case due to repeated linear scans of inorder
bruteForce.space: O(n) for recursion and the output structure
